opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think the big shift is that the models are now good enough to actually start from somewhere useful. If you go back a few years, people tried applying RL to language tasks, and the problem was that the policy you started with was so weak that you'd almost never sample a good trajectory. If you never see a reward, there's nothing to learn from. You're just exploring in this enormous space of possible token sequences and getting zeros back.

With today's pretrained models, plus some instruction tuning, the base policy is already pretty competent. When you ask it to solve a math problem or write a piece of code, some fraction of the time it gets it right. That fraction might be small, maybe ten or twenty percent on a hard task, but that's enough signal. RL can then take those successful attempts and push the model to do that more reliably. So in a way, pretraining solved the exploration problem for us, which was always the hardest part of RL.

The second piece is verifiable rewards. For a lot of domains we care about, like math, coding, and certain kinds of structured reasoning, you can check the answer automatically. Does the code pass the unit tests? Does the final answer match? You don't need a learned reward model that can be gamed, and you don't need humans labeling every output. That makes it cheap to generate a lot of reward signal, and it's much harder for the model to hack.

And then there's the infrastructure and the algorithms. Things like GRPO simplified the setup quite a bit. You don't necessarily need a separate value network; you sample a group of responses, compare them against each other, and use that as your baseline. Combine that with much better inference engines for fast rollouts, and the whole loop becomes something a small team can actually run, not just a big lab.

So it's really the combination: strong priors from pretraining, rewards you can verify, and simpler, more efficient tooling. Together they've moved RL from something that was theoretically appealing for language models to something that's genuinely practical, and I think we're going to see a lot more people, including smaller companies, using it to specialize models for their own tasks.

r001.rationale: It explains that pretrained models already produce some successful attempts, giving RL reward signal and reducing the need to explore blindly.

r002.rationale: It describes GRPO’s group comparisons and lack of a separate value network, but does not characterize it as largely similar to existing RL algorithms with incremental modifications.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks, Sam, great to be here. I think the short answer is that the pretrained model has already done most of the hard work for you.

If you go back to classic RL, say robotics or the Atari-style stuff, you were starting from a randomly initialized policy. The agent has no idea what the world looks like, what actions mean anything, so you spend an enormous amount of compute just getting it to produce behavior that's even slightly better than noise. Exploration was the whole problem, and the reward signal was so sparse that you basically needed to hand-craft shaping rewards to make any progress at all.

With a large language model, your starting policy is already incredibly competent. It knows language, it knows how to write code, it has some notion of math and reasoning. So when you set up an RL loop, say you ask it to solve a math problem and you check the final answer, it already gets things right some meaningful fraction of the time. That means you have a reward signal to learn from on day one. You're not exploring from scratch, you're sharpening something that already exists, and that changes the whole economics of RL.

The second piece is that verification has gotten cheaper in a lot of the domains people care about. Math problems have answers you can check. Code has unit tests. Even for things like agentic tasks, you can often write down a programmatic check of whether the task was completed. Once you have a verifiable reward, you don't need the fragile reward model that might get gamed, you can just optimize directly, and the model is strong enough to actually make use of that signal.

And then the third thing, honestly, is that the tooling and the algorithms have simplified a lot. Things like GRPO-style methods where you sample a bunch of completions, score them, and push toward the better ones, that's conceptually very simple compared to where RL was ten years ago. It's not magic. It's a well-understood recipe, and a lot of the painful instability has been engineered away because people have been iterating on it at scale.

So when you put those together, a strong prior, cheap verifiable rewards, and simpler algorithms, RL stops being this research curiosity and becomes something you can actually run as a product team. That's really why I think we're seeing it everywhere right now.

r001.rationale: The response says a pretrained LLM is already competent, gets answers right from the start, and is being sharpened rather than exploring from scratch.

r002.rationale: The response calls GRPO conceptually simple and a well-understood recipe, but does not say it is largely similar to existing RL algorithms with incremental modifications.

astra-6.text:
I think a big part of it is that we’re starting from a much stronger model. Traditionally, with reinforcement learning, you might start with a policy that’s essentially random, and it has to discover useful behavior through exploration. That can be incredibly expensive, especially when the reward is sparse.

With a pretrained language model, you already have a lot of useful behavior available. The model understands language, has acquired knowledge, and can generate plausible solutions. So reinforcement learning can focus on making those solutions better rather than discovering everything from scratch.

And in some domains, you can get a very concrete reward. If the model writes code, you can run tests and see whether it works. That gives you a feedback loop where you can sample solutions, evaluate them, and reinforce the successful ones. You still have challenges around reward design and training stability, but having that strong starting point makes a huge difference.

r001.rationale: It says pretrained language models already have useful behavior and knowledge, allowing RL to improve solutions instead of discovering everything through exploration from scratch.

r002.rationale: The response does not mention GRPO or characterize its relationship to existing reinforcement learning algorithms.

sol-6.1.text:
I think a big part of it is that we’re starting from a much stronger model. You’re not asking reinforcement learning to learn language or reasoning from scratch. The model already has a lot of useful capabilities from pretraining, and RL gives you a way to steer those capabilities toward an outcome.

And in domains like coding or math, you can often check that outcome. Does the code pass the tests? Is the answer correct? You can have the model generate a solution, evaluate it, and use that feedback to improve. That makes the reward signal much more concrete.

You still have challenges around exploration and making sure the model isn’t exploiting the reward. But having a capable starting point, together with tasks where you can verify success, makes reinforcement learning much more practical.

r001.rationale: The response says pretraining gives the model useful capabilities and a strong starting point, but it does not clearly explain that this reduces trial-and-error exploration.

r002.rationale: The response does not mention GRPO or characterize its relationship to existing reinforcement learning algorithms.
